summary: Specifies operations and management requirements for MPLS and for applications of MPLS such as pseudowire voice and virtual private network services. The requirements were gathered from network operators with extensive MPLS experience. The document is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: It lists what network operators need so they can check that a label-based network is healthy and find problems fast.

subtitle: What network operators told the IETF they need to find, diagnose and measure faults in MPLS networks.

tldr.problem: Operators running MPLS networks had no common list of what operations and management (OAM) tools must do to find and fix broken label switched paths (LSPs).
tldr.mechanism: The RFC collects requirements from experienced operators: automated defect detection, path tracing, path characterization, service level measurement, alarm handling, management interfaces and per-LSP accounting.
tldr.outcome: It proposes no mechanism. It is an Informational requirements list meant as a base for tool development and for guiding existing tools.

today: RFC 4377 is an Informational document and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself proposes no mechanism; it points to LSP ping (RFC 4379) only as an example of probe-based detection.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 4377 describes requirements for user and data plane Operations and Management (OAM) for Multi-Protocol Label Switching (MPLS), and for applications of MPLS such as pseudo-wire voice and virtual private network services. The requirements were gathered from network operators who have extensive experience deploying MPLS networks.

The RFC says plainly that no specific mechanisms are proposed to address the requirements. The goal is a commonly applicable set for the most common service provider MPLS networks at the time of writing. The set can be a base for network management tool development, guide the evolution of existing tools, and shape the OAM functions that are part of protocols used in MPLS networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a list of everything a bus company needs from its tracking tools. This RFC is that list for label-based networks. It does not build the tools.

sections.title: Defects and Latency Terms
sections.content:
A defect is any error condition that prevents a Label Switched Path (LSP) from functioning correctly, for example loss of an Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) path or an interrupted path for a traffic engineering (TE) tunnel. In multi-vendor or multi-provider operation, the parties need agreed definitions of when a path is broken and when it is not.

The RFC also defines the delay terms used later. Node latency is the sum of transmission, processing and queuing/buffering latency. One-hop delay is the fixed delay to reach the next hop (propagation, transmission and processing latency). Minimum path latency is the sum of the one-hop delays from ingress to egress, and variable path latency is the variation in the delays, otherwise known as jitter.
sections.plainLanguage: A defect is just a path that has stopped working properly. The delay words describe where time is lost on the trip: on the wire, at each stop, and waiting in line.

sections.title: Detecting and Diagnosing Broken Paths
sections.content:
Detection of a broken LSP MUST NOT need manual hop-by-hop checks of each router. It must be automated and run at an operator-specified frequency from the start of the LSP. The time to detect a defect plus the time for an operational support system to react must fit within the service level agreement (SLA). Detection time bounds should be synchronized between tools so test results are not ambiguous.

An ICMP-based ping sent through an LSP can give wrong answers, both positive and negative. ICMP packets are routable and can fall out of the LSP, giving a false positive, and they may not hash to the same equal-cost multi-path (ECMP) choice as the data traffic. Because LSPs are unidirectional, a check that needs an MPLS return path can wrongly report a working forward LSP as broken, so detection mechanisms SHOULD offer multiple return options, such as IP. The OAM packet MUST follow the customer data path exactly, including across ECMP permutations.

For diagnosis, the RFC requires isolating the failed link or node, best done with a path trace that returns the LSRs and links used by an LSP. The trace SHOULD handle nested (recursive) LSPs, MUST be able to diagnose LSP mis-merging by comparing expected and actual forwarding, and MUST support ECMP. Path characterization reveals details of forwarding operations, such as pipe or uniform TTL models, load-spreading permutations and stack operations at penultimate hop routers.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators want a robot that checks every road a delivery truck might take, from the start, and can say which stop is broken. A quick test that takes a different road would give the wrong answer.

sections.title: Measuring Service Quality and Handling Alarms
sections.content:
Mechanisms are required to measure the aspects of an SLA: latency, packet loss, jitter, and defect-free forwarding (the service is either available or it is not). Measurements can be independent of user traffic or a hybrid of user traffic and OAM probing. The ability to measure jitter, delay, latency and loss MUST be available, and any method SHOULD measure latency with minimal impact on network resources.

Operators MUST be able to configure OAM parameters, including how often OAM functions run. Probes with mismatched frequencies can cause flapping in cases such as mis-branching, so probe rates should be synchronized or probes should self-identify their rate, for instance by negotiating a rate when bootstrapping.

Network elements MUST provide alarm suppression, either discarding superfluous alarms or aggregating them. Because several MPLS applications may react to the same defect (for example layer-3 VPNs over TE tunnels), mechanisms are required to coordinate responses. An LSR that interworks another technology over MPLS MUST translate an MPLS defect into that technology's native error, for example ATM Alarm Indication Signal (AIS) cells for an emulated ATM virtual circuit. Recovery from faults SHOULD be automatic, and faults SHOULD be found by the operator before customers notice.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators also want to know how fast and how reliable the service is. When something breaks, they want one clear alarm instead of a hundred, and the fix to start by itself.

sections.title: Management Interfaces and Accounting
sections.content:
Wide deployment of MPLS needs common information models for managing OAM. The RFC points to the standard MPLS MIB modules (RFC 3813, RFC 3812, RFC 3814) but notes gaps in OAM coverage, so MIB modules for new protocol functions or tools are required. The ability to detect denial of service attacks on the data or control planes MUST be part of any security management related to MPLS OAM.

For per-LSP accounting, providers need traffic data for network design, for verifying service level specifications and for inter-AS services. Accounting is needed at the ingress, at intermediate routers (per ingress and egress pair) and at the egress. All routers measuring an LSP need a common identifier that MUST be unique to each LSP. To measure merged LSPs, a router MUST be able to tell the source of each flow apart. Per-LSP accounting SHOULD at least be done at the edges of the LSPs and of the MPLS domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators want the same kind of dashboard on every brand of equipment, and a counter for how much traffic each path carries so they can bill and plan.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Mechanisms built to meet these requirements must prevent unauthorized use, and MUST give operators a way to prevent denial of service attacks if the mechanisms themselves are used in an attack.

LSP mis-merging has security implications beyond being a network defect, and some of its possible causes, due to MPLS label stacking, are new to MPLS. Diagnostic and path characterization functions extract a lot of information about network construction that the operator MAY consider private.
sections.plainLanguage: The tools that look inside the network could be misused, so they need locks. They also reveal how the network is built, which an operator may want to keep private.
